- That deformation produces high strain rates, local adiabatic heating/jetting that disrupts surface oxides and contaminants, and intimate metal-to-metal contact.
- Bonding arises from a combination of mechanical interlocking and solid-state metallurgical bonding (cold welding), enabled by the cleaned, highly deformed contact zone; the same mechanism joins subsequent layers to build up a coating or part.
- The critical velocity and resulting deposit quality depend on material, particle size and temperature, and substrate condition.

Cold spray uses high-speed gas expansion to accelerate solid powder particles so that their kinetic energy produces solid-state bonding on impact.

Gas dynamics (how the jet is produced and accelerates particles)
- Compressed process gas expands through a converging–diverging (De Laval) nozzle to produce a high-velocity, often supersonic, jet. The achievable gas velocity is set by the stagnation pressure/temperature, nozzle geometry and the gas thermodynamic properties (specific heat ratio and molecular weight).
- Particles are injected into this high-speed flow and accelerate by aerodynamic drag. The drag force is Fd = ½ Cd A ρg (vg − vp)² and the particle acceleration a = Fd/mp (mp = particle mass). Because mp ∝ ρp d³ and A ∝ d², smaller and lower-density particles accelerate much faster; acceleration also increases with gas density and vg.
- Particle velocity therefore lags the gas velocity and is determined by residence time in the nozzle/jet, particle size and density, drag coefficient, and the local gas conditions. Standoff distance and shock/expansion structures in the jet also affect the particle speed arriving at the substrate.

Particle impact and deposition (how bonding occurs)
- Deposition occurs only when impact velocity exceeds a material-dependent critical velocity. Below that, particles rebound; above it, impact kinetic energy causes intense, localized plastic deformation.
- At impact the particle and near-surface substrate material undergo severe plastic deformation and very high strain rates. This can produce adiabatic shear, localized surface jetting, rupture or removal of oxide films, and exposure of fresh metal surfaces that enable intimate metal–metal contact and metallurgical bonding (plus mechanical interlocking).
- Repeated impacts build up a dense, low-porosity coating through consolidation and cold welding of particles. Very low thermal input means particles remain solid (no melting) and original microstructures and phases are largely preserved.
- Deposition efficiency rises rapidly above the critical velocity and then plateaus; if particle velocity is too high relative to substrate/material properties it can cause substrate erosion or particle fragmentation instead of deposition.

Key practical dependencies and caveats
- Critical velocity and the bonding mechanism depend on particle material, oxide films, particle size/morphology, substrate hardness/temperature, gas type, pressure and temperature, nozzle design, and standoff distance.
- Lighter gases and higher gas temperature/pressure generally increase particle velocity (but also cost and practical limits). Controlling residence time and nozzle flow quality is essential to deliver particles above the critical velocity without causing erosion.

In short: cold spray converts gas-dynamic energy (high-velocity jet) into particle kinetic energy; when particle impacts exceed a critical kinetic-energy threshold they plastically deform, remove surface films, and form solid-state metallurgical bonds to produce a consolidated coating.

Because aluminum powder is very soft and tends to stick, smear and "cold‑weld" to metal nozzle walls, polymer (plastic) nozzles are used to avoid or delay that fouling. Compared with conventional stainless‑steel or carbide nozzles, plastic nozzles give these practical and process benefits:

- Much lower nozzle fouling/caking: polymer surfaces have lower wettability/adhesion for soft Al and do not promote metal‑to‑metal transfer and build‑up the way hard metal walls do, so throat/divergent‑section clogging is reduced.  
- Longer continuous run times / more stable gas flow: reduced buildup keeps the gas jet geometry stable and avoids frequent stops to clear blockages.  
- Ability to run more aggressive spray conditions for Al: because fouling is reduced, operators can use higher gas temperatures and/or parameters that increase particle deformability and velocity, improving deposition efficiency, deposit density, cohesion and adhesion.  
- Lower replacement/repair impact: polymer nozzles are cheaper and easier to replace as sacrificial parts; using them avoids damage to expensive metal nozzles caused by Al adhesion.  

Key caveats and trade‑offs:
- Polymer nozzles wear faster from high‑velocity particle erosion and have an upper temperature limit (polymer thermal stability), so they must be replaced more often and cannot be used for the highest‑temperature/highest‑velocity regimes.  
- Nozzle material affects thermal and flow fields; geometry and polymer choice influence particle acceleration and lifetime, so results are process‑dependent.  
- Alternatives (e.g., high‑density graphite or specially coated/engineered metals) exist and may be preferred depending on lifetime, temperature and performance needs.

In short: plastic nozzles are used to prevent Al sticking/clogging and so enable more productive, stable aluminum cold‑spray runs, at the cost of reduced nozzle life and temperature limits.

Short answer: Particle impact velocity is one of the primary controls on cold‑spray microstructure. It determines whether particles adhere or rebound, the extent and localization of plastic deformation, and thus porosity, interparticle bonding, dislocation density, grain size (refinement), residual stress, and possible phase changes. Increasing velocity (within the process window) generally produces denser, better‑bonded, more heavily deformed and finer‑grained microstructures; excessive velocity can cause substrate erosion, cracking, or unwanted phase/thermal effects.

Key mechanisms and outcomes by effect of velocity

- Deposition threshold:
  - Below the critical velocity: particles largely rebound or plastically deform only slightly; feedstock microstructure is mostly retained; deposits are discontinuous, porous, and show distinct particle–particle interfaces.
  - Above the critical velocity: sufficient impact energy produces solid‑state bonding (cold welding), particle flattening and continuous coating formation.

- Extent and localization of plastic deformation:
  - Higher impact velocity → higher strain rate and peak stress at impact → extensive plastic flow at the particle rim and contact zone (jetting/peening).
  - Results in oxide/contaminant expulsion at the interface (clean metallic contact) and larger bonded area per particle.

- Dislocation multiplication and work hardening:
  - Higher velocities produce very large dislocation densities and work hardening in impacted zones; hardness and strength of the deposit increase locally.

- Grain refinement and dynamic processes:
  - Severe localized deformation can drive ultra‑fine grain formation via severe plastic deformation and dynamic recrystallization in the bonding/near‑surface regions of particles. In some systems, very high strain rates can induce localized amorphization or phase transformations.

- Interface morphology and porosity:
  - Low velocity → clear, unbonded interfaces, higher porosity.
  - Increasing velocity → reduction in interfacial porosity, fewer oxide‑decorated boundaries, more continuous metallic bonding. However, microstructure remains heterogeneous: highly deformed rims versus less‑deformed cores.

- Residual stress and damage:
  - Higher velocities increase residual stresses (often compressive near surface but complex through thickness) and may cause cracking, delamination, or substrate erosion if velocity is excessive relative to material toughness and substrate condition.

- Material‑dependent and practical caveats:
  - Exact velocity thresholds and resulting phenomena depend strongly on material properties (hardness, ductility, melting point), particle size/shape, substrate condition, impact angle and temperature. Some low‑melting or chemically active materials can experience local impact fusion at very high energy, altering microstructure and bonding.

Practical implication: choose particle velocity to be above the material‑specific critical velocity but within a window that maximizes interfacial jetting and severe plastic deformation (for bonding and grain refinement) while avoiding substrate damage, excessive residual stresses, or unwanted phase changes.

Direct answer: Lower glass transition temperature (Tg) generally makes polymer powder deposition by cold spray easier and more efficient. Lower-Tg polymers (or particles/substrates heated toward/above Tg) soften and plastically deform at the very high strain rates and local temperatures produced by impact, which promotes intimate contact, mechanical interlocking, polymer chain entanglement/interdiffusion at the interface, and therefore higher deposition efficiency and a wider deposition window. Higher-Tg (glassy) polymers remain stiff and brittle under the same conditions, so they require higher impact energy to achieve bonding, are more prone to fracture or rebound, and show lower deposition efficiency and a narrower window of successful process parameters.

Mechanisms (concise)
- Plasticity and adiabatic softening: when local heating/strain raises the polymer toward Tg, modulus drops and plastic flow at the interface increases bonding.  
- Mechanical interlocking / entanglement: softer material more readily conforms and mixes with substrate polymer chains, increasing cohesion/adhesion.  
- Brittle response at T < Tg: limited plastic deformation leads to rebound, cracking, or weak adhesion.  
- Rate dependence: Tg and polymer response shift with strain rate — polymers can behave effectively “glassier” at the extremely high strain rates in cold spray, so a lower equilibrium Tg helps ensure a ductile response under dynamic loading.  
- Localized heating and thermal diffusion: poor thermal conductivity confines heating to the interface; whether that local rise reaches Tg depends on particle/substrate properties and impact energy.

Key caveats and practical points
- Tg is one important factor but not the only determinant — impact velocity, particle temperature, particle size, crystallinity/molecular weight, substrate roughness/chemistry, and strain-rate effects also control deposition.  
- Heating the substrate or particles toward Tg can reduce required impact velocity and improve deposition, but overheating (or exceeding melting for semicrystalline polymers) may change the intended solid-state character or introduce defects.  
- Some material pairs show an upper-velocity failure mode (adhesive failure) even if Tg is low; optimal deposition requires tuning velocity/temperature within a deposition window.

Practical guidance (short)
- Prefer lower-Tg polymers for easier deposition or preheat particles/substrate toward Tg to increase efficiency.  
- Account for strain-rate-induced stiffening (effective Tg shift) when selecting Tg targets — aim for a comfortable margin so the material will behave plastically under impact.

Direct answer: powder morphology strongly controls both powder flowability (feed consistency, feeder/nozzle performance) and deposition efficiency (in‑flight acceleration, impact deformation, and bonding). Morphology influences these outcomes through aerodynamic drag, contact mechanics, surface state, and internal structure; the effects are material- and parameter-dependent and often involve trade‑offs.

Key effects and mechanisms

- Flowability and feeding
  - High sphericity and smooth surfaces improve bulk flowability, reduce hopper bridging, and give stable mass feed rates and consistent shot-to-shot dosing.
  - Irregular, angular, porous, or agglomerated particles increase interparticle friction and cohesion, raise the Carr index/tap–loose density spread, and can cause blockages, erratic feeding, and nozzle wear.
  - Satellite particles, high surface roughness, and agglomerates increase effective surface area and cohesion, degrading feedability.

- In‑flight behavior and velocity
  - Irregular/angular particles typically have higher aerodynamic drag coefficients than spheres, so under the same gas conditions they often accelerate to higher in‑flight velocities and/or exhibit different trajectories.
  - Spherical particles have lower drag, so they generally reach lower velocities for a given gas jet and size; to compensate they require higher gas energy, smaller size, or altered nozzle conditions.
  - Morphology-driven differences in orientation and rotation (torque) can change impact angle and local strain distribution on impact.

- Impact deformation and bonding (deposition efficiency)
  - Deposition in cold spray requires high strain, high strain‑rate plastic deformation to break surface oxides and form metallic bonding. Morphologies that promote symmetric, high‑strain flattening on impact favor bonding.
  - Angular/irregular particles often show greater effective flattening at the same velocity (lower critical velocity) because of higher kinetic energy transfer and stress concentrations, improving deposition efficiency for ductile metals.
  - Spheres may require higher velocities to reach the same degree of deformation; they can be less likely to bond at lower process energies and more likely to bounce or simply erode the substrate.
  - Agglomerated, porous, or brittle morphologies can fracture on impact, producing cracked, porous coatings or substrate erosion rather than cohesive deposits; internal porosity reduces momentum transfer and effective bonding.
  - Surface satellites and roughness can increase local oxide coverage and hinder intimate metal–metal contact, reducing deposition efficiency despite higher mechanical interlocking in some cases.

- Combined/composite powders and cermets
  - Heterogeneous morphologies (metal matrix with hard ceramic fragments, crushed blends, sintered agglomerates) complicate behavior: hard inclusions resist deformation, causing substrate erosion or poor bonding unless the ductile phase fraction and morphology support sufficient local plasticity.
  - Agglomerates may break up in flight, giving mixed behaviors and inconsistent coating microstructures.

Practical implications and selection guidance

- If stable, high-throughput feeding and minimal feeder/nozzle problems are primary, choose high‑sphericity, narrow‑size distribution powders; accept that process energy may need to be increased to obtain deposition.
- If maximizing deposition efficiency at lower gas energy is required (and feeder handling can be managed), irregular/dendritic powders can be advantageous because they accelerate better and often have lower critical velocities.
- Avoid or preprocess highly porous/agglomerated powders (deagglomeration, heat treatment, milling) unless intentionally spraying composites; control satellite content and surface oxides.
- Match powder morphology to material ductility and intended coating: brittle or hard phases typically need ductile carriers or specially engineered agglomerates to enable deposition.

Key caveat
- The net effect of morphology depends strongly on particle size, material mechanical properties, surface chemistry/oxide, and the chosen gas/nozzle/temperature settings. Morphology rules are directional—optimum choice must be validated for each material and process window.

Because cold spray bonding depends on high‑strain‑rate plastic deformation and material flow at the particle/substrate interface, hard brittle ceramic particles that do not plastically deform have much lower chances to form the intimate mechanical/metallurgical contact that produces durable deposition. In short: ceramics don’t flow, so they don’t bond.

Key reasons (technical):

- Bonding mechanism mismatch: Cold spray bonding requires localized plastic flow, jetting/oxide fracture, and dynamic recrystallization at the impact zone. Ductile metal particles undergo these processes and form strong mechanical and often metallurgical bonds; non‑deforming ceramics cannot produce that interfacial flow or jetting.

- Energy partitioning: The particle kinetic energy must be dissipated into plastic work and localized heating to generate bonding. For ceramics that energy is instead spent on elastic rebound, brittle fracture of the particle (or abrasive erosion of the substrate) rather than productive plastic deformation and bonding.

- Poor intimate contact and oxide disruption: Ceramic impacts do not fracture surface oxides or close gaps the way metal particle jetting does, so real contact area and interfacial intimacy remain low, reducing adhesion.

- Mechanical retention only: When ceramics are retained, it is usually by being mechanically trapped in a ductile metal matrix that deforms around them rather than by direct bonding. That makes incorporation efficiency dependent on the metal fraction and local packing rather than on direct particle adhesion, so overall retention of ceramic feedstock is lower.

- Strain/hardness mismatch and critical velocity: Hard ceramics require much higher impact energy (higher "critical velocity") to embed; below that they bounce or erode the substrate. Achieving those conditions is often impractical or damages the system.

Caveats and ways to improve retention:
- Mixing ceramics with a ductile metallic binder (pre‑agglomerates or powder blends) or using very high particle velocities / appropriate substrates can increase ceramic incorporation.
- Vacuum/supersonic processes, engineered agglomerates, or alternative solid‑state methods can deposit ceramics more effectively, but the baseline physical limitation remains: lack of plasticity makes ceramic deposition inherently less efficient than ductile metals.

Because polymers are thermally and mechanically sensitive, low‑pressure cold spray (LPCS) gives a gentler route to metallization: it reduces both the thermal load and the particle impact energy so metal can be deposited without melting or degrading the polymer substrate.

Key points
- Low thermal input: LPCS uses lower gas temperatures/expansion work than high‑pressure processes, so the substrate sees much less heat and is protected from melting, softening beyond recovery, chemical degradation or oxidation that higher‑temperature sprays can cause.  
- Reduced impact energy/erosion: lower particle velocities decrease the risk of abrasive erosion, macroscopic deformation or chain scission in the polymer. Particles are more likely to embed, deform locally and form mechanical interlocks rather than gouging the surface.  
- Enables deposition of softer/low‑critical‑velocity powders: metals with lower critical velocities (or powders that can be partially softened) will bond at LPCS conditions without imparting destructive energy to the substrate.  
- Lower residual stress and distortion: milder impact reduces built‑in stresses that can delaminate coatings or warp thin polymer parts.  
- Preserves conductivity and chemistry: the solid‑state nature and lower temperatures limit particle oxidation, helping electrical continuity where required.

Important caveats
- LPCS typically gives lower deposition efficiency, weaker interparticle cohesion and thinner/more porous coatings than high‑pressure cold spray; coatings on polymers often need surface preparation, interlayers, or post‑treatments (heat, anneal, plating) to reach target adhesion and conductivity.  
- High‑strength, high‑critical‑velocity metals are difficult to deposit directly by LPCS without damaging the polymer; process selection and powder choice must be matched to the substrate’s thermal/mechanical limits.

Short answer
Deposition efficiency falls as the nozzle is tilted away from normal because the particle velocity component perpendicular to the surface (the component that produces the severe plastic deformation and bonding) is reduced. There is a threshold (a material- and particle-size-dependent critical angle) below which the normal component is too small to reach the critical impact condition and deposition ceases.

Mechanism (concise)
- Bonding in cold spray is controlled by the normal component of particle impact velocity relative to a material-dependent critical velocity. Tilting the spray reduces that normal component while increasing the tangential component.  
- Reduced normal velocity → less plastic deformation, lower contact pressure and temperature rise, more rebound and sliding, and therefore lower probability of bonding.  
- Increased tangential component → more particle rebound or lateral displacement (erosion/skip), asymmetric build-up and gaps aligned with spray direction.  
- Because particles have a size/velocity distribution, larger (slower) particles lose bondability first as angle increases; this produces a gradual loss of deposition efficiency (a “transient” region) until a critical angle where no particles deposit.

Typical effects on deposit properties
- Maximum deposition efficiency near normal incidence.  
- As angle decreases from near-normal, deposition efficiency drops (often rapidly once you pass an intermediate range).  
- Off-normal impacts can increase local interfacial shear and in some cases raise single-particle bond strength, but bulk deposition efficiency and coating growth rate generally decline.  
- Off-normal deposition tends to increase porosity, asymmetry of thickness, and gaps between layers; near-normal impacts give higher flattening, lower porosity and more uniform thickness.

Practical implications
- To maximize deposition efficiency keep the nozzle as near-normal as practical, or compensate for off-normal work by increasing particle kinetic energy (higher gas temperature/pressure, shorter standoff, smaller particles) so the normal component still exceeds the critical condition.  
- For complex geometries, plan toolpaths, multiple passes, or angled fixturing to avoid sustained low-angle impacts.

Caveat
- The exact critical angle and the rate of efficiency loss depend on particle material, size distribution, substrate, and process energy—so quantify for your material/process before assuming numeric limits.

Short answer
Particle velocity is the primary driving parameter for bonding in cold spray: it controls the kinetic energy and momentum delivered at impact, and therefore whether a particle will plastically deform, generate interfacial jetting and local heating (adiabatic shear), disrupt surface films, and form a metallurgical/mechanical bond rather than rebound.

Key technical points

- Energy and momentum control
  - Kinetic energy (½mv²) supplies the work to produce plastic deformation and heating; momentum (mv) governs penetration/impulse and compaction of the contact zone. Both determine the extent of interfacial disruption and intimate contact needed for bonding.

- Critical velocity
  - For each material/particle size/temperature combination there is a threshold (critical) impact velocity below which particles tend to rebound or poorly adhere and above which bonding becomes probable. There are separate effective critical velocities for the first layer (particle→substrate) and for later layer growth (particle→particle).

- Bonding mechanisms activated by sufficient velocity
  - Severe, high-rate plastic deformation at the interface.
  - Localized temperature rise and adiabatic shear instability that produces local softening and material jetting at the interface.
  - Mechanical removal or breakup of oxide/contamination films and creation of fresh metal-to-metal contact enabling metallurgical bonding.

- Dependencies
  - Critical velocity depends on material properties (ductility, strength, melting point), particle size, particle temperature, and substrate condition. Increasing particle temperature or reducing particle size generally lowers the required velocity.
  - Spray angle and particle morphology also affect the effective normal component of velocity and therefore bonding.

- Effects of velocity magnitude
  - Below critical: low deposition efficiency, high rebound, weak/adhesive-free contacts.
  - Around/just above critical: good bonding via plastic flow and jetting; increasing deposition efficiency.
  - Excessively high velocity: may further improve bonding up to a point but can cause substrate erosion, excessive work hardening/residual stress, particle fragmentation, or reduced build quality (overheating or jetting damage).

- Practical implications
  - Process setpoints (gas temperature/pressure, nozzle design, feedstock selection) are chosen to deliver particle velocities just above the material-specific critical window to maximize deposition efficiency and mechanical integrity while avoiding damage.
  - Monitoring and controlling the particle velocity (e.g., optical Doppler sensors or calibrated process maps) is fundamental to reproducible cold spray AM.

Caveat
- Velocity alone does not guarantee bonding; it must be considered together with particle size, temperature, oxidation state, substrate preparation, and impact angle.

Short answer
- Increasing stand-off distance typically reduces deposition efficiency and weakens particle–particle and particle–substrate cohesion, but the effect is material- and powder-dependent and can be non‑monotonic (an optimum distance often exists).

Why (mechanisms)
- Particle kinetics: longer flight time means particles experience the expanding/decaying gas jet and often lose axial momentum and/or miss the high-velocity core. Lower impact velocity reduces plastic deformation on impact and therefore reduces ability to form strong mechanical/metallurgical bonds → lower deposition efficiency and weaker cohesion.
- Thermal state: particles cool as the gas expands. Lower impact temperature reduces thermal/strain softening and flattening on impact, further lowering bonding and increasing porosity.
- Flow features: at very short distances bow/shock structures near the substrate can decelerate particles and cause rebound/erosion (reducing effective deposition). Increasing distance can reduce bow‑shock effects, so for some powders (especially fine or dense particles) deposition efficiency can first increase with distance before falling as particles slow/cool.
- Particle properties: light or fine particles decelerate and cool faster (more sensitive to increased distance) than large/heavy particles, which may continue accelerating or retain kinetic/thermal energy longer. Thus the distance dependence differs with size, density and critical velocity.
- Secondary effects: longer distances tend to increase porosity and surface roughness and can increase rebounding/shot‑peening of the previously deposited layer, reducing cohesive strength.

Practical implications / guidance
- There is typically an optimal stand-off specific to powder, particle size distribution, gas/nozzle flow and substrate; outside this window deposition efficiency and cohesion fall off.
- Determine particle impact velocity/temperature vs distance (e.g., PDV or modeling) and compare to the material’s critical velocity to pick the best distance.
- For fine/light powders, favor shorter distances (but avoid bow‑shock zone); for coarse/heavy powders a longer distance may be tolerated or beneficial up to the optimum.
- Evaluate coating porosity, interparticle bond strength and adhesion vs stand-off distance rather than relying on a single rule.

Key caveat
- The trend (decrease vs non‑monotonic behavior) depends strongly on powder size/density and nozzle/flow geometry; do not assume monotonic decrease for all material/powder combinations.

Direct answer:
The main thermal-spray families are (1) combustion-based flame processes (including conventional flame spray and detonation gun), (2) fuel/oxygen high‑velocity processes (HVOF), (3) electric‑arc/plasma processes (atmospheric and vacuum plasma spray, plasma-transferred wire arc), (4) wire-arc spray, and (5) suspension/solution and specialized variants. In all of these conventional thermal sprays the feedstock is heated to or near the molten/semi‑molten state and particles are propelled onto the substrate where they deform, flatten into splats, and build a lamellar coating.

How cold spray relates:
- Cold spray (also called cold gas dynamic or kinetic spray) is part of the spray/coating family but it is fundamentally different in energy and bonding mechanism. Powder is kept solid (well below melting) and is accelerated to very high velocity by rapid gas expansion.  
- Deposition is driven by particle kinetic energy: upon impact particles undergo extremely high strain‑rate plastic deformation, jetting, adiabatic shear and mechanical interlocking that produce metallurgical/physical bonding rather than solidification of a melt.  
- Key consequences: minimal thermal exposure of feedstock and substrate (reduced oxidation, phase changes, thermal distortion and residual stresses), excellent retention of starting powder chemistry and microstructure, dense coatings with low oxide content, and good capability for repairing or joining temperature‑sensitive materials and multilayers.  
- Limits relative to molten sprays: cold spray favors ductile metals/metallic powders (brittle ceramics are difficult to deposit unless embedded in a ductile matrix), requires reaching a material-specific critical particle velocity for bonding, and may need thicker build-up or post-treatment for some property targets.

Summary: cold spray complements conventional thermal sprays by providing a solid‑state, kinetic route to dense, low‑oxidation metallic coatings and repairs where thermal damage is a problem, while traditional thermal processes remain preferable when true melting, ceramic splat formation, or certain bond/structure outcomes from molten deposition are required. Key tradeoffs are material depositability, required particle velocity, and thermal vs. mechanical bonding mechanisms.

Typical particle size
- Cold spray powders are normally in the micron range ≈ 10–100 µm.  
- For most metals the frequently used band is about 20–60 µm; low‑density metals can be pushed to larger sizes (~up to 100 µm). Particles <~10 µm or >~100 µm are generally difficult to accelerate and deposit efficiently.

Carrier/propulsive gases
- The two most common gases are nitrogen (cost‑effective) and helium (lower molecular weight → higher achievable particle velocity).  
- Argon and compressed air are sometimes used for specific materials/processes; choice depends on desired particle velocity, reactivity/oxidation risk, and cost.  

Key caveats
- Powder size distribution and morphology (spherical, narrow PSD) strongly affect deposition; optimal size depends on material density and the spray system/nozzle and gas choice.

Short answer: because plasma spray exposes WC–Co particles to much higher temperatures and longer high‑temperature residence times (and often more oxidizing conditions) than lower‑temperature, higher‑velocity processes. That drives carbon loss (decarburization), dissolution of WC into molten Co, evaporation/oxidation of binder, and rapid melt/quench effects that produce W‑rich/decomposed phases, porosity and poor splat bonding — all degrading coating microstructure.

Mechanisms (technical):
- High particle temperatures and long in‑flight residence time accelerate thermal decomposition of WC (WC → W2C → W) and enable carbon to be lost as CO/CO2 (oxidation) or to diffuse out of the carbide.
- The cobalt binder often melts in the plasma; molten Co greatly increases diffusion rates and allows WC to dissolve into a Co–W–C liquid, promoting further carbide dissolution and redistribution of W and C.
- Oxidation and evaporation of binder (and entrapped gases) create pores and depress wetting/flow of droplets, increasing porosity and defects.
- Rapid quenching of molten or partially molten droplets produces non‑equilibrium microstructures: amorphous or supersaturated binder, fine recrystallized W‑rich phases, brittle intermetallic carbides — these reduce toughness and cohesion.
- Plasma flames typically impart lower particle velocities than HVOF/cold spray; lower impact deformation/flattening reduces mechanical interlocking and splat bonding, so even molten/solidified deposits are less well consolidated.
- Combined, these effects give coatings with higher porosity, unmelted and partially decomposed particles, weak intersplat boundaries, and altered (W‑rich, decarburized) phase chemistry — all reducing hardness uniformity, toughness and wear performance.

Key caveats:
- Severity depends on plasma power, gas composition, stand‑off distance, particle size and feedstock condition; process tuning can reduce but not eliminate decarburization.
- Lower‑temperature/high‑velocity processes (HVOF, detonation gun) or solid‑state methods (cold spray) are preferred when minimizing WC decomposition and maximizing coating density and cohesion.

Short answer
- Increasing propellant gas pressure and/or temperature tends to raise particle impact velocity and particle temperature, which increases deposition efficiency by making it more likely particles exceed the material‑specific critical velocity and undergo the severe plastic deformation needed for bonding.  
- However, both parameters have trade‑offs: too little pressure/temperature gives no bonding; too much can cause particle/substrate damage, excessive heating (thermal softening, oxidation, phase changes) or particle fragmentation that reduce coating quality and can lower effective deposition efficiency.

How it works (mechanisms)
- Particle kinetic energy control: gas stagnation pressure and nozzle exit conditions set the gas jet momentum and therefore particle acceleration. Higher pressure → higher particle velocity → higher impact kinetic energy (KE ∝ v^2) → greater plastic deformation and higher probability of exceeding the critical velocity required for bonding.  
- Temperature effects on gas dynamics: raising the propellant temperature increases gas enthalpy and sound speed in the nozzle; this can produce higher exit Mach numbers and higher particle velocities for a given pressure.  
- Particle thermal softening and ductility: preheating particles raises their temperature at impact, lowering flow stress and critical velocity so ductile bonding is easier for low‑ductility materials.  
- Residence time and drag: higher pressure (and to a lesser extent temperature) changes gas density/viscosity and particle drag/hang‑time in the jet; this affects acceleration and the particle size range that can be carried efficiently.  
- Detrimental effects at high settings: excessive velocity or temperature can cause substrate erosion, particle fracture, work‑hardening or rapid strain localization that prevents bonding, oxidation or phase transformations from elevated particle temperature, and increased porosity from thermal softening — all of which reduce useful deposition efficiency or coating integrity.

Dependence on material and particle size
- The optimal pressure/temperature window is highly material dependent. Ductile metals generally need lower conditions to reach critical velocity; hard, low‑ductility metals, alloys and ceramics require higher gas energy (or a lighter gas) and/or higher temperature to achieve bonding. Particle size and density also change acceleration and optimal settings.

Practical guidance
- Aim to set pressure and temperature so that the particle impact velocity is slightly above the material’s critical velocity (maximize bonded fraction without inducing damage).  
- If deposition is poor, first increase gas pressure (raises velocity) or temperature (reduces critical velocity and increases velocity), monitoring for signs of thermal damage, oxidation, particle fracture, or substrate erosion.  
- Optimize together with particle size, stand‑off distance and carrier gas choice because their combined effect determines actual particle velocity and temperature at impact.

Caveat
- There is no universal pressure/temperature recipe — settings must be tuned to the powder, substrate, particle size distribution and desired coating properties.

Increasing propellant gas temperature and pressure generally reduces cold‑spray coating porosity — up to an optimal window — because both raise particle impact velocity and (for temperature) can partially soften particles, which increases plastic deformation, interparticle/interfacial contact and bonding, and void closure.

Mechanism (brief):
- Higher pressure → greater mass flow and gas momentum → higher particle acceleration and momentum on impact → more plastic deformation and densification.
- Higher gas temperature → higher gas sound/flow velocity and warmer particles → higher impact velocity and easier particle deformation (reduced flow stress), improving bonding and reducing entrapped porosity.

Key caveats and limits:
- There is a critical impact‑velocity threshold for adhesion; below it porosity is high. Increasing T and P helps reach and exceed that threshold.
- Beyond an optimal range, further increases can be detrimental: excessive velocity can cause particle fragmentation, substrate erosion, or high residual stresses/peel‑off; excessive particle thermal softening or recrystallization can change deformation behavior and in some materials increase porosity or weaken the deposit. The net effect depends on material ductility, particle size, gas type and standoff distance.
- Other processing variables (particle size distribution, nozzle geometry, standoff distance, carrier gas species) interact with T and P and must be optimized together.

Practical rule of thumb:
- Increase T and P to reliably exceed the material’s critical velocity to reduce porosity, then tune down or adjust other parameters to avoid over‑acceleration or thermal effects that introduce new defects.

Because cold spray deposits are formed by extreme solid-state plastic deformation rather than melting, the as-sprayed microstructure and interfaces are typically mechanically bonded, highly work‑hardened, defected, and diffusion‑limited. Post‑deposition heat treatment is therefore often required to convert that as‑sprayed structure into a robust, stable coating with the required properties. Key reasons and mechanisms:

- Improve interparticle/metallurgical bonding: elevated temperature activates atomic diffusion across particle–particle and particle–substrate interfaces (sintering-like processes), closing gaps and turning mechanical contacts into metallurgical bonds.

- Reduce porosity and heal microdefects: diffusion and boundary migration promote neck growth and elimination of voids, microcracks and weakly bonded “splat” boundaries, increasing cohesion and load transfer.

- Relieve residual stress and recover ductility: recovery and (if used) recrystallization reduce dislocation density and residual stresses produced by severe plastic deformation, restoring ductility and improving fatigue resistance and adhesive strength.

- Microstructure homogenization and precipitate control: heat treatment can dissolve, redistribute, or reprecipitate second phases (or relieve non‑equilibrium segregation), tailoring strength/ductility and corrosion behaviour.

- Improve functional properties: lower electrical/thermal resistance, better corrosion resistance and wear performance follow from reduced porosity, improved bonding and microstructural equilibration.

Key caveats:
- Heat treatment conditions must be tailored to the coating alloy and substrate; some alloys (precipitation‑hardened grades) can lose strength if over‑annealed, and substrates may be damaged or change properties.  
- For in‑service repairs, heat treatment may be impractical or undesirable; localized methods (laser, induction, FSP, HIP) can be used to limit effects.  
- Not every application needs full heat treatment—requirements depend on target mechanical/functional performance.

In short: post‑spray heat treatment transforms a mechanically consolidated, work‑hardened, porous deposit into a metallurgically bonded, less stressed, and often more ductile and durable coating.

Direct answer: lighter, low‑molecular‑weight process gases (e.g., helium) produce higher particle velocities in cold spray and, for a given powder and nozzle setup, generally yield denser deposits with lower porosity. Heavier gases (e.g., nitrogen or air) produce lower particle velocities and—unless compensated by higher temperature/pressure or other parameter changes—tend to give higher porosity and lower deposition efficiency.

Why (mechanism)
- Gas thermodynamics set the maximum flow velocity: the nozzle-exit gas speed scales with the gas sound speed a = sqrt(γ·R·T). Lower molecular weight (higher specific gas constant R) and favorable γ give higher a for the same stagnation temperature → higher achievable gas velocity and higher aerodynamic acceleration of particles.
- Particle acceleration depends on relative gas velocity, gas density/viscosity, particle size and time in the flow. Higher gas velocity (and appropriate gas density/drag) produces larger particle speeds at impact.
- Particle impact velocity controls bonding: above a material-dependent critical velocity particles undergo large plastic deformation, jetting and cold-welding, closing voids and producing low-porosity deposits. Below that critical velocity bonding is poor and porosity is high.

Practical effects on porosity and deposit quality
- As particle impact velocity increases (via lighter gas or higher gas temperature/pressure), porosity typically decreases and deposit hardness, cohesion and adhesion increase — often nonlinearly once velocities pass the critical-deposition threshold.
- For many material systems there is an optimum: extremely high gas temperature or velocity can induce thermal softening/over-deformation, increased erosion of previously deposited material, or higher residual stress, which can locally raise porosity or produce defects.
- Gas density and viscosity also matter: heavier gases can transfer momentum differently; in some cases increasing pressure/temperature with a heavier gas can partially compensate for lower molecular weight, but usually at higher energy/cost penalties.

Operational trade-offs
- Helium (or low‑molecular‑weight gases) improves velocity and lowers porosity but is costly; nitrogen is cheaper and commonly used but often requires higher pressure/temperature or different powder/nozzle choices to reach similar deposition quality.
- Blended gases are used to balance cost and performance: even modest fractions of light gas can significantly raise particle velocity and reduce porosity.
- Final porosity always depends on combined factors (particle size/morphology, material strength, nozzle, standoff, spray angle). Gas choice is a primary lever but must be optimized with the rest of the process window.

Key caveat: the quantitative effect of gas on particle velocity and porosity is material‑ and geometry‑dependent; use particle velocity measurements or modeling to select gas and settings that exceed the material’s critical velocity without causing deleterious effects.

Short answer
- In most cold-spray systems, raising the propellant gas temperature increases deposition efficiency and reduces coating porosity — but only up to an optimal window.  
- Beyond that window the trend can reverse or plateau: excessive heating can promote detrimental effects (oxidation, softening/partial melting, poorer peening or rebound/erosion), which can reduce DE and/or increase porosity.

Why (mechanisms)
- Higher gas temperature → higher gas velocity and density/enthalpy for given pressure → higher particle exit velocities and higher particle temperatures.  
- More particles exceed the material’s critical velocity for bonding, so a larger fraction adhere on impact → higher deposition efficiency.  
- Higher impact velocity and elevated particle temperature increase severe plastic deformation, flattening and intimate metal–metal contact, enhancing bonding and filling interparticle voids → lower porosity.  
- Elevated particle temperature can also lower flow stress (easier deformation), promote dynamic recrystallization at high strain rates, and improve interparticle metallurgical contact, all contributing to densification.

Key caveats and exceptions
- Material- and feedstock-dependent: hard, work‑hardening materials, ductile metals, oxophilic powders, and different particle sizes respond differently.  
- Too high temperature can:
  - Approach or exceed local melting, producing defects or undesirable microstructure;  
  - Increase oxidation or other gas–particle reactions that impede bonding and increase porosity;  
  - Soften particles such that subsequent peening from following particles is reduced, possibly leading to looser packing or trapped voids in some cases;  
  - Cause increased particle rebound or nozzle/plasma flow changes that reduce effective impact conditions.
- Other parameters (gas type and pressure, particle size distribution, nozzle geometry, standoff distance, and substrate condition) interact with temperature; optimal temperature must be determined for each material/process set-up.

Practical guidance
- Use temperature to raise particle velocity toward but not far beyond the material’s optimal bonding regime (critical velocity window).  
- Optimize gas temperature together with pressure, particle size and standoff distance; verify porosity and DE experimentally for the specific powder and application.

Short answer: Increasing oxide scale thickness on feedstock powders raises the critical particle velocity (Vcr) needed for bonding in cold spray. Thicker, more adherent oxide layers act as a barrier to the plastic deformation and jetting required for clean metal–metal contact, so particles must impact faster (deliver more kinetic energy) to crack, delaminate or peel off the oxide and expose fresh metal for bonding.

How and why (technical, concise)
- Mechanical barrier: Oxide scales are typically stiffer and more brittle than the underlying metal. A thicker oxide increases the effective surface rigidity and reduces the extent of particle plastic deformation at a given impact energy. That suppresses jet formation and reduces real contact area with the substrate/previously deposited particles.
- Fracture and delamination demand energy: Bonding requires oxide segmentation, cracking, local delamination or total peel-off so that fresh metal contacts are exposed. Thicker/tougher oxides need more impact energy to achieve these failure modes, so Vcr increases.
- Reduced bonded area and adhesion: If oxide remains intact or only partially segmented, bonded contact area is small and adhesion strength falls even if some bonding occurs. Practically this lowers deposition efficiency and may require still-higher velocities to obtain acceptable coatings.
- Dependence on oxide properties and powder features: The effect scales with oxide thickness but is modulated by oxide adhesion to metal, fracture toughness, porosity/structure (friable vs compact), particle size/shape and impact angle. A friable or poorly-adhered oxide can fragment more readily and thus produce a smaller Vcr increase than a dense, strongly adhered oxide of the same thickness.

Practical implications and mitigations
- Expect a monotonic (often roughly linear in many studies) rise in Vcr with oxide thickness/oxygen content for a given material and spray condition. The magnitude of the rise is material- and oxide-dependent.
- To lower Vcr and improve deposition efficiency: reduce oxide thickness (chemical/mechanical cleaning), engineer a more friable oxide layer, or increase particle impact energy (higher gas temperature/pressure or different carrier gas) while accounting for other process constraints.

Caveat: Exact change in Vcr for a given increase in oxide thickness depends on the specific metal–oxide system, oxide mechanical properties and the spray conditions; quantification requires material-specific data or modeling.

Short answer: At a fixed impact velocity, increasing particle diameter generally increases single‑particle adhesion capability (higher probability of bonding), up to practical limits. Larger particles deliver more momentum and localized heating/plastic deformation at the contact and are therefore more likely to exceed the size‑dependent conditions for oxide fracture and metal‑to‑metal bonding; very small particles are more likely to rebound or require collective/in‑situ peening to build a coating.

Key technical reasons (scaling and mechanisms)
- Kinetic energy, momentum and contact loading
  - Mass ∝ d^3 so kinetic energy ∝ d^3 (at fixed v). Contact area scales roughly ∝ d^2, so energy (and momentum) per unit contact area scales ~ d. Larger particles therefore produce larger localized stresses and work density at the interface, promoting plastic flow and bonding.
- Contact time and strain rate
  - Impact/contact time ~ d/v, while characteristic strain rate ~ v/d. Smaller particles experience higher strain rates (v/d) and shorter contact times, which can limit the development of the large plastic flow patterns needed for interfacial bonding.
- Thermal softening vs heat diffusion
  - Thermal diffusion time ∝ d^2/α (α = thermal diffusivity). The ratio of diffusion time to impact time ∝ d·v/α. Larger particles behave more adiabatically during impact (heat stays local), so plastic work produces greater local temperature rise and softening that helps oxide fracture and bonding. Small particles lose heat faster during the short impact and therefore soften less.
- Oxide film fracture and metallurgical contact
  - Bonding requires sufficient local plastic deformation to break surface oxides and expose fresh metal. Larger particles are more effective at creating the required interfacial shear and jetting/peeling; small particles often fail to do so at the same v.
- Limits and exceptions
  - Very large particles at a given v can cause substrate erosion, poor flattening, or brittle fracture; adhesion does not increase indefinitely with size.
  - Very fine particles can still contribute to coating formation via in‑situ peening (many impacts) or by filling gaps, but their single‑particle adhesion probability at the same v is lower.
  - Material properties (yield strength, work hardening, oxide character), particle temperature, and substrate hardness shift these trends and change the size at which behavior transitions.

Practical implication: At constant spray velocity, expect a lower size bound below which particles will mostly rebound and a range of larger diameters with much higher single‑particle adhesion; choose particle size with regard to desired deposition mode and beware excessive size causing substrate damage.

Standoff distance (SoD) is the gap between the cold‑spray nozzle exit and the substrate (or previously deposited layer). It is a key geometric process parameter because particles continue to accelerate, cool and interact with the gas flow after leaving the nozzle; SoD therefore controls their state at impact.

General effects on coating formation
- Particle kinetics: SoD changes particle velocity and temperature at impact. Shorter distances tend to preserve higher velocities/temperatures from the nozzle exit; longer distances allow more gas‑particle interactions, drag and cooling that reduce velocity and temperature. Whether a particle reaches the material’s critical deposition velocity depends on SoD.
- Deposition efficiency and thickness: Because impact velocity is a primary driver of bonding, SoD strongly affects deposition efficiency and resulting coating build rate/thickness. Too long a SoD generally reduces efficiency; too short a SoD can also reduce efficiency (see bow‑shock effects below).
- Bonding, porosity and microstructure: Lower impact velocity/temperature (from excessive SoD) reduces plastic deformation and metallurgical/adiabatic bonding, typically increasing porosity and weakening interparticle/substrate bonds. Moderate SoD that maximizes velocity and softening tends to improve densification.
- Flow disturbances and bow shock at short SoD: If the nozzle is too close, a bow shock or flow perturbation can form ahead of the substrate, creating drag and decelerating particles (especially fine/low‑mass particles), which reduces deposition and can increase rebound. Short SoD can also expose the substrate to higher gas temperatures and cause local heating.
- Surface effects and mechanical finishing: SoD influences shot‑peening and strain‑hardening contributions from rebounding particles; these can affect residual stress, hardness and near‑surface work hardening.
- Material/powder dependence: The optimal SoD depends on particle size, density, critical velocity, nozzle design and gas conditions. Effects can be non‑monotonic for some powders (e.g., heavy/large particles may have a different optimal SoD than light/fine ones).

Practical implication: SoD must be optimized for a given nozzle, gas/pressure/temperature, powder and substrate to balance particle velocity, temperature, oxidation risk and flow effects; optimization is normally done by modeling and/or controlled experiments.

Fluence is the laser energy delivered to a surface per unit area. It is the fundamental measure of how much energy a given spot on the material receives and is usually expressed in J/cm2 or J/mm2.

Key definitions and formulas
- For a single laser pulse: fluence H = Epulse / Aspot (J/area).
- For a continuous-wave beam scanned across a surface: H = P · tinteraction / Aspot = (P/Aspot) · tinteraction, where P is power (W), Aspot is the beam spot area, and tinteraction is the time the beam illuminates a given surface point. For a linear scan, tinteraction ≈ dspot / vscan (dspot = characteristic beam dimension along scan, vscan = scan speed).
- Irradiance (power density) I = P/Aspot (W/area), and H = I · tinteraction. For pulsed trains, cumulative fluence = fluence per pulse × number of overlapping pulses.

Why fluence matters for laser post‑treatment of cold‑sprayed coatings
- Controls melting vs. solid‑state response: fluence determines whether the coating surface remains in the solid state (annealing, recrystallization, plastic flow) or partially/fully melts (glazing, melt-pool formation). That dictates densification mechanisms and microstructure evolution.
- Sets melt‑pool depth and extent of consolidation: the energy per unit area required to heat and melt a given thickness scales with fluence (accounting for material density, specific heat, latent heat and heat losses). Correct fluence can seal surface porosity and weld particle boundaries; excessive fluence melts too deeply and may cause dilution with substrate or subsurface defects.
- Controls porosity, interparticle bonding and corrosion/wear performance: adequate fluence reduces surface porosity and eliminates weak interparticle boundaries, improving mechanical integrity and corrosion resistance. Insufficient fluence leaves porosity and poor bonding.
- Determines surface finish: higher fluence generally gives stronger smoothing/polishing (reflow) but can also produce ripples, resolidification defects or increased roughness if mis‑matched to scan strategy.
- Influences residual stress, cracking and distortion: higher delivered energy increases thermal gradients and cooling rates, raising tensile residual stresses and risk of cracking, delamination or substrate damage—critical for cold‑sprayed coatings on temperature‑sensitive substrates.
- Affects microstructure and properties: fluence controls grain growth, dissolution/formation of phases, hardness changes and potential oxidation or phase transformations through peak temperature and time at temperature.
- Dependent on absorption and thermal diffusion: incident fluence is not the same as absorbed energy—absorptivity (wavelength, surface condition) and thermal properties (conductivity, diffusivity) determine heating efficiency and melt depth. Thermal diffusion during tinteraction spreads heat beyond the illuminated area.

Practical implications and control
- Tune fluence via power, spot size, scan speed, pulse energy/repetition rate and overlap. For scanned processing, reduce scan speed or increase power to raise fluence; increase spot size or speed to lower it.
- Consider per‑pass fluence and cumulative fluence from overlapping passes or pulses; plan overlap to achieve intended cumulative energy without local overheating.
- Target the minimum fluence that achieves the desired densification/relief to avoid substrate heating, dilution or cracking.
- Account for beam profile (Gaussian vs top‑hat), absorptivity changes during heating, and the coating/substrate thermal coupling when predicting melt/thermal response.

In short: fluence quantifies how much laser energy a surface point receives and is the primary parameter that determines whether and how the cold‑sprayed coating will melt, densify, polish, or be damaged. Proper control of fluence (and its interaction with beam size, scan speed, overlap and material absorption) is essential to achieve the intended post‑treatment results without introducing defects.

Direct answer: Helium typically produces substantially higher particle impact velocities and—other things equal—greater particle heating than nitrogen. This arises from fundamental gas-property differences (molecular weight, specific heat ratio, thermal conductivity) that raise the gas exit speed and the gas-to-particle heat transfer when helium is used.

Key points (technical, concise)

- Gas exit speed dependence:
  - Gas velocity at nozzle exit scales like Vg = M·sqrt(γ Rspec Tg) where Rspec = Runiv/MW. Helium’s much lower molecular weight and higher specific‑heat ratio (γ) give a larger sqrt(γ Rspec Tg) term than nitrogen for the same Mach number and stagnation temperature. Result: higher Vg with He.
- Particle acceleration:
  - Particle velocity is driven by the gas velocity and opposed by particle inertia; smaller or lower‑density particles accelerate closer to Vg. Because He yields a higher Vg, particles reach higher impact velocities with He under identical nozzle/stagnation conditions.
- Particle temperature (heating):
  - Helium has higher thermal conductivity and, combined with higher gas velocity, increases convective heat transfer to particles. That tends to raise particle temperature (and substrate/interfacial temperature) relative to nitrogen for identical operating conditions.
  - Particle heating also depends on particle size, residence time in the hot/high-speed jet, and gas temperature: small particles heat faster and can equilibrate more with the gas; larger particles remain cooler.
- Practical implications:
  - Higher impact velocity with He helps reach critical velocities for deformation/bonding of hard/high‑strength materials and improves deposition efficiency and particle deformation.
  - Helium’s stronger heating can promote plasticity/jetting at impact but may also increase surface reactions if oxygen is present.
  - Nitrogen can be tuned (higher stagnation temperature/pressure, different nozzle design) to approach the same particle velocity and/or particle temperature, but this often requires higher energy input and may still be limited relative to He for some materials.
- Caveats:
  - Absolute particle velocity and temperature are functions of many coupled parameters (stagnation pressure and temperature, nozzle geometry, particle size/density, stand-off distance). The He vs N2 effect is a dominant but not exclusive factor.
  - Economic and safety trade‑offs: helium is more expensive and often recovered/recycled in production; nitrogen is cheaper and commonly used where its performance suffices.

Bottom line: for identical gun/nozzle/stagnation conditions helium gives higher gas exit speed → higher particle impact velocity and generally greater particle heating (especially for small particles). Nitrogen can be compensated by higher temperature/pressure or gun/ nozzles adjustments, but helium remains the more effective route to higher velocities and faster particle heating.

The critical velocity is the material- and condition-dependent threshold impact speed that a cold‑spray particle must exceed to transition from simple rebound to permanent bonding on impact. It is commonly defined experimentally as the impact velocity at which deposition efficiency reaches about 50%, but conceptually it is the minimum kinetic-energy condition required to activate the deformation and interfacial mechanisms that produce adhesion.

Why it is essential
- Mechanism activation: exceeding the critical velocity converts kinetic energy into severe plastic deformation, localized heating and shear at the particle–substrate (or particle–particle) interface. This enables phenomena such as jetting that remove oxides/contaminants, intimate metal–metal contact, mechanical interlocking and, in many cases, metallurgical bonding (dynamic recrystallization/strain‑induced bonding).
- Coating initiation and growth: there are effectively two thresholds — one for the first layer (particle-to-substrate) and one for subsequent layers (particle-to-deposit). Particles below the appropriate critical velocity simply rebound, so no coherent coating forms; particles above it build and densify the coating rapidly as velocity increases.
- Process window control: the critical velocity defines the lower bound of the productive spray window. Staying above it but below higher velocities that cause erosion or substrate damage is necessary for high deposition efficiency, low porosity, and good bond strength.

Key dependencies and practical implications
- Critical velocity depends on material properties (yield strength, hardness, ductility), particle size and morphology, oxide/contamination, particle temperature, substrate properties, gas/nozzle conditions and impact angle.
- It can be lowered (i.e., easier bonding) by increasing particle temperature or ductility, reducing particle size, or changing substrate conditions; conversely, harder/less-ductile materials require higher velocities.
- Too high an impact velocity can move the process out of the productive window into erosion and reduced deposition efficiency.

In short: critical velocity is the minimum impact speed required to produce the plastic-deformation and interfacial processes that cause particles to stick and build a dense cold‑spray coating; it governs whether deposition occurs and strongly controls coating quality.

Increasing the propellant gas temperature generally increases cold‑spray coating density (reduces porosity). Higher gas temperature raises particle kinetic energy and particle temperature for the same pressure, which increases particle velocity and promotes stronger plastic deformation and mechanical interlocking at impact — increasing deposition efficiency and producing denser, better‑bonded deposits. 

The practical maximum gas temperature is set by operational limits rather than deposition physics. Key constraints are nozzle and system hardware (nozzle material softening, erosion or fouling, heater and seal ratings) and powder stability (oxidation, thermal softening or partial melting that causes agglomeration/clogging). These limits determine the usable maximum temperature and create a trade‑off: beyond an optimal temperature, thermal softening, oxidation or nozzle problems can degrade coating quality.

The critical velocity (Vc) in cold spray is the threshold particle impact speed above which a particle undergoes the required severe, high‑strain‑rate plastic deformation (adiabatic shear, jetting and oxide break-up) to produce metallurgical/mechanical bonding to the substrate rather than rebounding. Vc therefore defines the lower bound of the usable “deposition window” (below Vc: rebound/erosion; above Vc but below an upper erosion velocity: deposition).

What Vc depends on (principal parameters and typical trends)
- Particle and substrate mechanical properties
  - Yield/tensile strength, hardness, strain‑rate sensitivity and work‑hardening: higher strength/harder materials generally raise Vc (more kinetic energy required to produce the necessary plastic flow).
  - Density and acoustic properties (speed of sound): acoustic impedance and sound speed influence shock/pressure generation; for matched materials Vc scales with bulk sound speed.
- Thermal properties and temperatures
  - Particle and substrate temperature and melting point, specific heat and thermal conductivity: preheating (higher particle impact temperature) softens the particle and reduces Vc; materials with higher melting/softening points or heat capacity typically require more energy (higher Vc).
- Particle geometry and condition
  - Diameter, shape and porosity: Vc shows a particle‑size dependence (commonly a power‑law relation); porous or irregular particles generally need higher Vc. Surface condition (oxide scale, contamination) increases Vc because oxide removal/breakup requires additional energy.
- Particle–substrate pairing and surface state
  - Material mismatch (ductile vs hard, adherent oxide layers), substrate roughness and compliance, and surface cleanliness influence bonding; cleaner, softer/matched pairs give lower Vc.
- Impact kinematics and environment
  - Impact angle (normal impact minimizes Vc; oblique increases it), and presence of oxidizing atmosphere (increases Vc by growing/maintaining oxides).
- Process variables (via their effect on particle state)
  - Gas type, pressure and temperature and nozzle design control achievable particle velocity and temperature and thus determine whether Vc is reached.

Representative functional form (qualitative)
- Models often reduce to an energy/pressure balance: Vc scales with sqrt(energy required to plastically deform and heat the particle / particle mass). Thus Vc increases with required plastic/ fracture strength terms and decreases with particle softening (higher Ti), and is inversely linked to particle density.

Key caveats
- Vc is not a single universal number — it is specific to the particle/substrate combination, particle size and temperature, surface condition and impact geometry, and must be determined or modeled for each system. There is also an upper erosion velocity (typically ~2–3×Vc depending on materials) that limits the useful window. Experimental or validated predictive models are required for accurate process setting.

Short answer: At fixed inlet (stagnation) pressure, raising the propellant gas temperature typically increases the particle velocity at the nozzle exit.

Why (mechanisms)
- More available enthalpy: higher stagnation temperature raises the gas specific enthalpy that can be converted to kinetic energy in the nozzle expansion, so the gas exit velocity increases.
- Higher speed of sound: a ∝ sqrt(T). For a given Mach number the gas velocity is larger when temperature is higher, so the flow can reach a higher absolute velocity.
- Particle heating: hotter gas raises particle temperature, softening particles and lowering their critical/deformation threshold so they couple more readily to the gas and deform more on impact.
- Net momentum transfer: although gas density at a given static pressure decreases with temperature (which tends to reduce drag force), the increase in gas velocity (and thus dynamic pressure and available momentum flux) usually dominates, so particle acceleration increases.

Important caveats
- The magnitude of the effect depends strongly on nozzle geometry, residence time, particle size/mass and gas species. Small particles accelerate more readily than large/heavy ones.
- Flow choking and mass-flow effects: for choked nozzles the mass flow and density change with temperature (mdot ∝ P0/√T0), so higher temperature can reduce mass flow even as local sound speed and gas exit velocity increase; this can alter particle loading and coupling.
- Diminishing returns and practical limits: beyond some temperature increases the particle velocity gain saturates and material/oxidation/safety limits constrain usable temperatures.

Net practical rule: increasing gas temperature at constant pressure is an effective, commonly used way to raise particle exit velocity and improve deposition, but the actual benefit must be evaluated for the specific nozzle, particle size and gas.

Direct answer:
Preheating the substrate generally improves bonding quality in cold spray of nanoparticles by raising the substrate surface temperature at impact, which increases local plasticity, promotes particle–substrate intimate contact and metallurgical bonding, and enlarges the mechanically interlocked/bonded area. However, benefits are balanced by increased surface oxidation, possible microstructural changes, and an optimal temperature window that depends on materials and process conditions.

Key mechanisms (how preheating helps)
- Thermal softening: higher substrate temperature lowers yield strength locally, so substrate material deforms more readily on particle impact. That increases contact area, promotes jetting/flow at the interface and reduces elastic rebound — all favoring stronger bonds.
- Enhanced adiabatic-shear/strain localization: warmer substrates make it easier for the high-strain, localized flow at the impact rim to occur, producing metal jetting and fresh metal–metal contact that fosters solid-state bonding.
- Increased atomic mobility: elevated interfacial temperature raises diffusion rates and contact intimacy, enabling more metallurgical (solid-state) bonding and faster neck growth between nanoparticles and substrate.
- Greater mechanical interlocking: substrate surface can plastically conform into asperities and particle clusters, increasing mechanical anchoring of the deposited layer.
- Compensates for low particle momentum: nanoparticles carry much less momentum per particle than larger powders; substrate softening mitigates this by allowing bonding with lower impact energy.

Main caveats and limits
- Oxidation/contamination: heating can thicken oxide films or adsorbed layers that act as barriers to metallurgical bonding. Net effect is a trade-off — beyond an optimum temperature oxidation may reduce adhesion.
- Temperature window and material dependence: the beneficial temperature range is material-specific. Too little heating gives marginal improvement; too much can cause excessive oxidation, grain growth in nanoparticles or substrate, thermal stresses, or microcracking.
- Surface condition interplay: substrate roughness, cleanliness, and thermal effusivity alter the effect. For example, roughness can either aid mechanical locking or hinder adiabatic jetting depending on scale and material.
- Process and particle-scale differences: because nanoparticles transfer heat and momentum differently than larger particles, the magnitude of improvement and the optimal preheat value differ — typically nanoparticles are more sensitive to substrate temperature.

Practical implication
Use controlled preheating to raise the substrate surface temperature into the range that maximizes thermal softening and interfacial atomic mobility while minimizing oxidation and detrimental thermal effects. Optimize experimentally for the specific particle–substrate pair and atmosphere.

Direct answer: particle velocity in cold spray is set by momentum transfer from the propellant gas to the particle, so it depends on gas properties that control gas velocity, density and drag, and on particle properties that control inertia and aerodynamic drag.

Key gas properties
- Gas molecular weight / specific gas constant: lighter gases (higher R, lower molecular weight) yield higher gas speeds for the same temperature and pressure (higher sonic and jet velocities).
- Gas temperature: raises gas sound speed and jet velocity (and heats particles), increasing acceleration and exit velocity.
- Gas pressure (stagnation pressure): increases gas density and mass flow, raising the drag force and particle acceleration.
- Gas density and viscosity: density (ρg ∝ p/T) determines available momentum per unit volume; viscosity (μg) and mean free path set the drag law and particle Reynolds number.
- Specific heat ratio (γ): governs expansion behavior through the nozzle and attainable Mach number/jet velocity.
- Compressibility / flow regime (Mach number, choked flow): determines nozzle performance and maximum gas velocity delivered to particles.

Key particle characteristics
- Diameter (d): primary control on inertia — mass ∝ d^3 while aerodynamic area ∝ d^2, so larger particles accelerate much more slowly. Smaller particles track the gas better and reach higher velocities.
- Density (ρp): heavier (higher density) particles have greater inertia and accelerate more slowly for the same drag force.
- Shape and sphericity (drag coefficient Cd): non‑spherical or angular particles have higher Cd and can either accelerate faster initially (if they present larger projected area relative to mass) or suffer more aerodynamic losses and dispersion; shape controls Cd(Re) and the effective projected area.
- Porosity / agglomeration / internal structure: porous particles or agglomerates behave as larger effective diameters (lower effective density or higher drag) and typically reach lower velocities or fragment.
- Size distribution and mass loading: polydisperse feedstock causes a spread of particle velocities; higher particle loading reduces gas velocity (momentum coupling) and lowers individual particle velocities.
- Surface roughness: alters drag and local flow separation, affecting acceleration and jet dispersion.
- Mechanical/thermal state (temperature, pre‑softening): does not directly set free‑flight velocity much, but particle heating by the gas can change density slightly and affects deformation/fragmentation on impact.

Useful relations (compact)
- Drag force: Fd = 0.5·Cd(Re, shape)·ρg·A·(ug − up)^2, with A ∝ d^2.
- Particle mass m ∝ ρp·d^3, so acceleration a = Fd/m scales roughly ∝ (ρg/ρp)·(1/d)·Cd·(u_rel)^2 (order‑of‑magnitude).
- Particle relaxation time (continuum/Stokes regime): τp ≈ (ρp·d^2)/(18·μg) (or more generally includes Cd corrections). Short τp → particle follows gas quickly; long τp → particle lags.

Caveats
- Real acceleration depends on nozzle geometry, available acceleration length (stand‑off), interparticle collisions, and the evolving relative velocity (u_rel) — so the simple scalings give trends but must be combined with nozzle flow and particle trajectory modelling for quantitative prediction.

Short answer
High-pressure gases are used to accelerate solid powder particles to very high (often supersonic) velocities so that their kinetic energy, not heat, produces bonding by severe plastic deformation and oxide-film disruption. Keeping the gas and particles well below melting prevents melting-related oxidation, phase changes, and large thermal stresses, producing dense, high-strength coatings that retain the feedstock’s original metallurgy.

How the choice (high pressure + low temperature) produces bonding
- Acceleration: High pressure (and a light carrier gas) through a supersonic nozzle gives particles the momentum/kinetic energy required to exceed the material’s critical velocity for bonding.  
- Solid-state bonding mechanism: At impact the particle undergoes extreme localized plastic shear (often via adiabatic shear instability) that fractures surface oxide films, produces fresh metal-to-metal contact and jetting, and causes mechanical interlocking with the substrate or underlying deposit.  
- No melting: Because particle and gas temperatures remain below melting, bonding is achieved without liquid-solid interfaces or resolidification.

How that choice influences coating integrity
- High cohesion and adhesion: Severe plastic deformation and oxide removal give strong particle–particle cohesion and particle–substrate adhesion (high bond strength).  
- Low porosity and high density: Plastic flattening and intimate contact produce dense deposits with low porosity compared with many thermal-spray processes.  
- Preserved metallurgy: Avoiding melting minimizes oxidation, decarburization, phase transformations, grain growth, and compositional changes—retaining original mechanical and corrosion properties of the feedstock.  
- Low residual tensile stresses: Because there is no melting and solidification shrinkage, thermal tensile stresses are much lower; residual stresses are usually compressive, which benefits fatigue and wear life.  

Key caveats and trade-offs
- Must reach the material’s critical velocity; insufficient pressure/velocity yields poor deposition.  
- Excessive impact energy can damage thin or soft substrates (erosion, embedding) or cause unacceptable work hardening.  
- Very hard/brittle powders or high-melting ceramics may be difficult to plastically deform and build thick dense coatings without special feedstock or process adaptations.  
- Higher gas pressures and hot preheating (still below melting) improve particle velocity but increase equipment/wear and operational cost; gas choice (He vs N2) affects achievable velocity.

In short: high-pressure, low-temperature gas flow shifts the process from thermal bonding to kinetic, solid-state bonding—producing dense, low-oxidation, mechanically robust coatings while avoiding melting-related degradation, provided particle velocities and feedstock/substrate combinations are properly matched.

Direct answer: Cold spray produces a dense, low‑porosity, defect‑poor coating microstructure formed in the solid state (no melting), preserving feedstock phase purity and retaining/refining grain structure through severe plastic deformation.

Brief technical explanation:
- Because particles impact and bond by high‑velocity plastic deformation rather than melting and solidification, interparticle interfaces are tightly consolidated with far fewer pores and oxide inclusions than conventional thermal sprays.
- The process preserves the original phases (avoids melting‑related phase transformations and oxidation) and can retain or produce very fine / work‑hardened (often nanoscale) grains instead of the coarse, cast/solidified microstructures typical of thermal spray.
Caveat: the degree of densification, phase retention, and grain refinement depends on material and process parameters (particle velocity, temperature, substrate preparation).

Direct answer: nozzle geometry and powder injection location control the gas flow field (Mach number, pressure, density, shocks, turbulence) and the particles’ exposure to that flow (residence time, slip velocity, heating and radial position). Those two factors therefore set the magnitude and spatial distribution of particle impact velocities and strongly influence deposition efficiency and spray footprint.

Key mechanisms and effects

- Nozzle geometry
  - Converging–diverging shape (throat, divergent section) determines gas acceleration and exit Mach number; higher effective expansion in the divergent section increases gas velocity and can raise particle speed.
  - Expansion ratio and divergent length control where and whether normal/oblique shocks form: poorly matched geometry moves shocks toward the exit or downstream, which creates local decelerations and non‑uniform particle velocities.
  - Throat area and exit area set gas density and drag history; a longer/appropriately sized divergent section can increase particle acceleration by extending the high-speed gas region, but excessive length lowers gas density and reduces drag force so particle acceleration can fall off.
